Brazilian genius Kaka fully deserves winning the 2007 World Footballer of the Year award. When AC Milan defeated Liverpool in the Champions League final in Athens, avenging their heartbreaking loss to the same team in Istanbul two years previously, it enabled Kaka to fulfill his dream of holding aloft Europe's premier trophy -- a winner's medal he fully deserved after a sublime 90-minute performance. Kaka's stock for both club and country has risen steadily since his move to the San Siro from Sao Paulo for a fee of just $8.5 million in the summer of 2003. Unlike many a Brazilian sporting genius, Kaka did not hone his skills on the beach or the streets of a favela shanty town. He was born into a comfortable middle class Brasilia family, where football was not the only hope of a bright future. However, it soon became clear that this particular boy had a very special skill and he was signed by Sao Paulo, after his family had moved there, at just eight years of age -- making his first team debut as an 18-year-old. Kaka's progress was soon picked up by his national team coach and Felipe Scolari named the graceful midfielder in his 23-man squad for the 2002 World Cup finals, earning him a winners' medal despite playing only 19 minutes of the tournament in a group match against Costa Rica. A year later, and Kaka was on his way to Milan. Within a month he had made the starting line-up and his 10 goals helped the Rossoneri lift the Scudetto and the European Super Cup. Throughout his career, Kaka has always possessed the innate ability to score goals -- his record for both club and country sees him average roughly a goal every three games. Yet to describe Kaka merely as a goalscoring midfielder would be doing him a massive injustice. Tall, elegant and blessed with astonishing skill, Milan and Brazil utilize Kaka's ability superbly. Milan coach Carlo Ancelotti soon recognized Kaka's genius, changing his team's system to a 4-4-1-1, playing the Brazilian behind a main target man. With Andrea Pirlo and Gennaro Gattuso holding the central midfield area, Kaka has a license to roam in behind the lone striker, be it Filippo Inzaghi, Ronaldo or Alberto Gilardino. And Kaka does this with devastating effect, running at the opposition with pace and power, finding defense-splitting passes or shooting from range with deadly accuracy be it from a dead-ball situation or open play. The fly in the ointment for Milan comes in the shape of their poor form this season. Although they have already reached the last 16 of the Champions League, the club are floundering in Serie A and face the unthinkable prospect of not qualifying for next season's competition unless they win the trophy. Real Madrid have coveted Kaka for the last two years -- expect the world transfer record to be smashed if Milan don't secure a place among Europe's elite. E-mail to a friend .

**Kaká’s golden year: Why Milan’s quiet genius stands above Ronaldo and Messi**

*December 2007 — Sports feature*

In a year overflowing with young brilliance, the world’s most compelling footballer was not the winger of whirring stepovers at Manchester United, nor the teenage phenomenon cutting through defenses in Barcelona colors.

It was the elegant Brazilian in red and black, the one who seemed to glide rather than run, the player who turned Europe’s most demanding competition into his own personal stage.

Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite — Kaká to the football world — has made the strongest case to be named World Footballer of the Year and Ballon d’Or winner in 2007. Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi may represent the future of the sport, but Kaká owned the present.

And he did it where greatness is most brutally measured: in the Champions League.

## Milan’s European leader

AC Milan’s 2006-07 season was complicated, imperfect and at times overshadowed by the aftershocks of the Calciopoli scandal that had rocked Italian football. Milan began the Serie A campaign with a points deduction and never truly looked like domestic title contenders.

But in Europe, Carlo Ancelotti’s side found its rhythm, experience and identity. At the center of it all was Kaká.

Milan had veterans everywhere: Paolo Maldini, Alessandro Nesta, Andrea Pirlo, Clarence Seedorf, Gennaro Gattuso, Filippo Inzaghi. But the decisive attacking force was Kaká, the player who transformed tight matches into open roads.

He finished as the Champions League’s top scorer with 10 goals, an extraordinary return for a player who was not a traditional striker. More importantly, his goals came with consequence.

Against Celtic in the last 16, he carried Milan through a tense tie with a brilliant extra-time winner at San Siro, driving from midfield before finishing with the calm of a forward. Against Bayern Munich in the quarterfinals, he scored and influenced the tempo of the tie. Then came the defining duel: Manchester United.

That semifinal was billed as a clash between two of the game’s great rising superstars: Kaká and Cristiano Ronaldo. Ronaldo’s United were marching toward the Premier League title, full of pace, swagger and attacking confidence. But over two legs, it was Kaká who left the deeper mark.

At Old Trafford, he scored twice in a 3-2 Milan defeat, including a remarkable solo goal in which he embarrassed United’s defense with movement, balance and composure. In the return leg at San Siro, Milan overwhelmed United 3-0 in the rain, and Kaká struck again, setting the tone for one of the club’s great European nights.

Then came the final in Athens, a rematch against Liverpool two years after the trauma of Istanbul. Milan won 2-1, with Inzaghi scoring both goals, but Kaká remained central to the triumph, supplying the pass for Inzaghi’s second and serving as the creative link that Liverpool struggled to fully contain.

The Champions League is not the only measure of a footballer, but in 2007 it is the decisive one. Kaká did not merely participate in Milan’s seventh European Cup. He drove them there.

## Why Kaká over Cristiano Ronaldo

Cristiano Ronaldo’s 2006-07 season was magnificent. He became Manchester United’s most explosive attacking player, scored freely from wide areas, won the Premier League, and was voted England’s top individual performer. His transformation from flashy prospect to ruthless match-winner was one of the stories of the year.

But the case for Kaká is stronger because the defining confrontation between them came on the biggest European stage — and Kaká prevailed.

Ronaldo dazzled domestically. Kaká dominated Europe.

In the Champions League semifinal, Ronaldo was dangerous, but Kaká was decisive. He played with a clarity and efficiency that separated him from the field. Every touch appeared to have purpose. Every run seemed timed to fracture a defensive line. Where Ronaldo still sometimes played with youthful excess, Kaká’s brilliance was already mature.

Ronaldo may be the most spectacular athlete in football. Kaká, in 2007, was the most complete big-game attacker.

## Why Kaká over Lionel Messi

Lionel Messi’s genius is already undeniable. His balance, acceleration and dribbling have invited comparisons with Diego Maradona, especially after his stunning solo goal against Getafe in the Copa del Rey — a run that looked like a modern echo of Mexico 1986.

But Messi’s year was not as complete as Kaká’s. Barcelona did not win the Champions League. They lost La Liga to Real Madrid. Messi’s gifts may be unmatched in their raw form, and his ceiling may be the highest of any player in the world, but 2007 belongs to achievement as well as promise.

Messi gave football glimpses of the future. Kaká delivered the year’s defining performances.

That distinction matters.

## From São Paulo to San Siro

Kaká’s rise has always carried a sense of grace, perhaps because his story differs from the familiar tale of Brazilian football hardship.

Born in Brasília in 1982 and raised in a middle-class family, Kaká grew up with strong religious faith and a grounded public image. His nickname came from a childhood mispronunciation of “Ricardo” by his younger brother, Rodrigo.

His career might have been derailed before it truly began. As a teenager, Kaká suffered a serious spinal injury in a swimming-pool accident, an episode he has often described as shaping his faith and perspective. He recovered, progressed through São Paulo’s academy, and emerged as one of Brazil’s brightest young midfielders.

He joined AC Milan in 2003, when many wondered whether he would need time to adapt to Serie A. Instead, he quickly made himself indispensable. In a league known for tactical discipline and defensive intelligence, Kaká’s directness was startling. He could receive the ball between midfield and defense, turn instantly, and accelerate into spaces that had not seemed to exist.

He helped Milan win Serie A in 2004 and became a key part of Ancelotti’s refined midfield structure. By 2005, he was already playing in a Champions League final. By 2007, he was the team’s attacking leader.

## The beauty of his game

Kaká’s style is unusual because it is both graceful and devastatingly direct.

He is not a dribbler in the Messi mold, weaving through traffic with tiny touches. Nor is he a winger like Ronaldo, built around tricks, explosive changes of direction and one-on-one showmanship. Kaká’s genius is in the long stride, the sudden burst, the perfectly weighted touch into space.

He plays like an attacking midfielder with the instincts of a sprinter and the finishing of a forward.

When Kaká runs at a defense, the field seems to tilt. He carries the ball with his head up, rarely appearing rushed, and defenders are forced into an impossible choice: step toward him and open a passing lane, or retreat and allow him to shoot. He can score from distance, slip passes into strikers, arrive late in the box, or break through the center of the pitch in a way few modern players can.

In Milan’s system, this made him priceless. Pirlo could dictate from deep. Gattuso could destroy. Seedorf could connect. Inzaghi could lurk. But Kaká gave Milan vertical force. He turned possession into penetration.

That was the difference between a fine side and the champions of Europe.

## The Real Madrid question

Naturally, a player at the height of world football attracts the attention of Real Madrid.

The Spanish giants have long been linked with Kaká, and it is easy to understand why. He has the glamour, the global appeal and the technical excellence traditionally coveted at the Bernabéu. For Madrid, still rebuilding its identity after the Galáctico era, Kaká would be more than a signing. He would be a statement.

Milan, however, have been firm in their insistence that he is not for sale. Kaká has also repeatedly spoken warmly of life at the club, where he is adored by supporters and trusted by Ancelotti. At San Siro, he is not simply another star. He is the symbol of Milan’s next generation, the bridge between the Maldini-era dynasty and whatever comes next.

Still, football’s economics are changing. If Real Madrid continue to circle, the speculation will not disappear. Kaká is exactly the kind of player capable of reshaping the balance of European power.

For now, though, he belongs to Milan — and Milan’s European crown belongs in large part to him.

## A worthy winner

The debate over the world’s best player is rarely settled by statistics alone. It is about timing, trophies, influence and memory. It is about who defined the year.

Cristiano Ronaldo had a brilliant season in England. Lionel Messi produced moments of breathtaking genius in Spain. Both may win this award in the future, perhaps many times.

But Kaká’s 2007 was complete.

He was the leading scorer in the Champions League. He was the best player in the competition’s decisive rounds. He inspired AC Milan past Manchester United and helped deliver revenge against Liverpool in the final. He combined elegance with efficiency, faith with ferocity, humility with match-winning authority.

In a year of emerging icons, Kaká stood tallest.

The Ballon d’Or is meant to honor the player who rose above all others. In 2007, that player wore No. 22 for AC Milan.

# Kaka: The Elegant Brazilian Who Rose Above Football’s New World Order

**MILAN —** In an era increasingly defined by speed, spectacle and commercial noise, Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite — known to the world simply as **Kaka** — has won football’s highest individual honour with a style that feels almost disarmingly pure.

The Brazilian playmaker was named **2007 FIFA World Player of the Year**, completing a remarkable sweep of the game’s major individual awards and confirming what the European season had already made clear: no footballer in the world had been more decisive, more graceful or more devastating than the AC Milan midfielder.

For Kaka, the award is the crowning recognition of a year in which he led Milan to the **UEFA Champions League title**, finishing as the competition’s top scorer and delivering the kind of performances that turn excellent players into enduring figures. For Brazil, it is another chapter in a long history of attacking geniuses. For Milan, it is vindication of a team built around intelligence, experience and moments of refined brilliance. And for world football, it marks a striking moment: at the height of the emerging Cristiano Ronaldo-Lionel Messi rivalry, the game’s throne belongs to a tall, soft-spoken Brazilian whose football is at once explosive and understated.

Kaka did not win because of volume alone. He won because of clarity. In the biggest matches of 2007, he made the complicated look simple and the simple look beautiful.

## The Year Kaka Took Control

The defining images of Kaka’s year came in Europe.

In the 2006-07 Champions League, Milan were not always the most fashionable team in the tournament. They were experienced, certainly, with Paolo Maldini, Alessandro Nesta, Andrea Pirlo, Clarence Seedorf and Filippo Inzaghi giving the club a formidable spine. But they were also seen by many as a side approaching the end of a cycle, a team carrying scars from the 2005 final in Istanbul and still navigating the aftershocks of Italian football’s Calciopoli scandal.

Kaka changed the mood.

He scored **10 goals in the Champions League**, more than any other player in the competition, and his influence extended far beyond the numbers. He was Milan’s accelerator, the player who could turn a conservative passage of possession into a direct threat within two strides. He did not dribble with the low centre of gravity of Diego Maradona or Ronaldinho, nor did he overwhelm opponents with stepovers and theatrical gestures. Instead, Kaka ran upright, almost serenely, the ball close enough to command but far enough ahead to invite acceleration.

When he surged into open grass, defenders often appeared to be chasing not a man but a decision already made.

His performance in the semi-final tie against Manchester United became the emblem of his campaign. At Old Trafford, Kaka scored twice in a 3-2 first-leg defeat, including a goal that will remain among the defining moments of his career. Splitting the United defence, he caused Gabriel Heinze and Patrice Evra to collide before calmly finishing past Edwin van der Sar — a sequence that combined pace, timing, composure and a faintly improbable elegance.

In the second leg at San Siro, Milan overwhelmed United 3-0 in the rain, with Kaka again setting the tone. It was one of the most complete European performances of the season, and it carried Milan into a final against Liverpool, a rematch freighted with the memory of Istanbul.

This time, Milan prevailed. In Athens, Inzaghi scored twice in a 2-1 victory, but Kaka supplied the decisive pass for the second goal — a perfectly weighted through ball that released the veteran striker behind the Liverpool defence. It was a classic Kaka contribution: quick, vertical, unforced, lethal.

By the time the final whistle blew, the Champions League had become not merely Milan’s redemption story, but Kaka’s coronation route.

## A Different Kind of Superstar

Kaka’s rise is distinctive not only because of what he does on the pitch, but because of what he seems to resist off it.

He is a global star without the sense of excess that often accompanies the status. His public manner is calm, courteous and devout. He speaks often about his Christian faith, famously wearing shirts bearing religious messages beneath his kit. In an industry drawn to controversy, image-making and constant self-projection, Kaka has presented himself with unusual restraint.

That restraint, however, should not be mistaken for softness.

On the field, Kaka is a devastating competitor. His game is built on sharp changes of rhythm, intelligent positioning and a rare ability to attack central spaces at speed. He is not a traditional Brazilian No. 10 in the narrow sense — not a static orchestrator operating entirely between midfield and attack. Nor is he simply a second striker. At his best, he is something between playmaker, runner and finisher: a modern attacking midfielder whose greatest weapon is the transition from thought to motion.

He receives, turns and goes. The move is often that direct.

Born on April 22, 1982, in Brasília and raised in São Paulo, Kaka came from a comfortable middle-class background, unusual among many Brazilian footballers whose origin stories are shaped by poverty and street football. Whether Milan can keep pace financially and athletically with the new powers of European football may determine how long that future lasts. But in 2007, there is no question that club and player have elevated each other.

## A Crown Earned in Motion

There are footballers who dominate by force of personality, others by statistical accumulation, others by the aura of genius. Kaka’s domination in 2007 was built on motion — the sudden, devastating act of carrying the ball through the heart of a match and changing its direction.

Football’s future is gathering around him. Ronaldo is rising. Messi is coming. Brazil is waiting. Milan are dreaming.

But for this year, and on this stage, the world belongs to Kaka — the elegant runner from Brazil who made Europe bend to his stride.

## The peak before the next era

In hindsight, Kaká’s 2007 triumph carries extra historical significance because it came just before the Messi-Ronaldo duopoly reshaped the meaning of individual dominance. For more than a decade afterward, the game’s top awards became almost exclusively filtered through their rivalry.

Kaká was the last player to win the Ballon d’Or before that era fully began.

That fact can sometimes make his victory feel like a bridge between ages. But it should not be seen as a footnote. Kaká did not win because Messi and Ronaldo were not yet ready. He won because he had produced a year worthy of the prize by any standard.

At his best, he was not merely keeping the seat warm for the next generation. He was the standard.

## A rightful winner

The 2007 World Footballer of the Year award belonged to Kaká because he combined the four qualities that define a truly worthy winner: elite performance, decisive impact, major trophies and unforgettable style.

He was the best player in the Champions League. He was AC Milan’s attacking soul. He produced against the strongest opponents. He elevated the biggest occasions. And he did it with a kind of grace that made even ruthless efficiency look effortless.

Football awards are often debated endlessly, and rightly so. They are subjective, shaped by timing, preference and memory. But some years feel clearer than others.

In 2007, Kaká’s case was overwhelming.

He was not just the rightful World Footballer of the Year. He was the player who made the game look pure, devastating and beautiful all at once.
